25432:
Joseph, Jacob's eleventh son and Rachel's firstborn, is the central figure of the longest continuous narrative in Genesis (chapters 37-50). Favored by his father and gifted with dreams of his family bowing before him, he provoked his brothers' hatred and was sold into slavery in Egypt. There he rose to manage the house of Potiphar, was falsely accused and imprisoned, and through his God-given ability to interpret dreams came to stand second only to Pharaoh.

Joseph's foresight preserved Egypt and the surrounding lands through seven years of famine, and the famine brought his brothers to him for grain. Rather than taking revenge, he tested them, discovered in Judah's offer to take Benjamin's place a changed heart, and revealed himself with tears. He moved Jacob's whole household to Goshen, setting the stage for Israel's growth in Egypt and the exodus.

The story is notable for how rarely God speaks directly; instead the narrator and Joseph himself discern God's hidden providence working through human evil and ordinary decisions. Joseph's words, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Gen 50:20), have become a classic statement of providence. His request that his bones be carried to Canaan expresses faith that God would keep the promise of the land (Heb 11:22).
25433: Joseph is the son of Rachel (Gen 30:22-24), loved more than his brothers (Gen 37:3), sold into Egypt (Gen 37:28), and in Potiphar's house the LORD is with him (Gen 39:2-3). He refuses Potiphar's wife (Gen 39:9), interprets dreams in prison and for Pharaoh (Gen 40-41), and is made ruler over Egypt at thirty (Gen 41:40-46). He marries Asenath, daughter of Potiphera priest of On (Gen 41:45), tests and forgives his brothers (Gen 42-45), settles his family (Gen 47:11), centralizes land ownership under Pharaoh during the famine (Gen 47:13-26), and dies at 110 (Gen 50:26). Psalm 105:16-22 retells his story as God's sending a man ahead. Stephen recounts it (Acts 7:9-16), and Hebrews praises his faith concerning his bones (Heb 11:22). Exod 1:8 notes a later king who did not know Joseph.

25435: Joseph is a major type of Christ: beloved of his father, rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, humbled and then exalted, and forgiving those who wronged him (Ambrose, *On Joseph*). Orthodox liturgy commemorates "Joseph the all-comely" during Holy Week.

Others argue for older roots. No Egyptian record names Joseph, and his historicity is debated.

25507:
Job is the central figure of the book that bears his name, a blameless and God-fearing man from the land of Uz who loses his wealth, children and health in a series of disasters. The reader is told what Job never learns: that his suffering follows a challenge in the heavenly court, where the accuser claims Job serves God only because God has blessed him. Job's initial response is famous for its resignation: "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

Most of the book, however, is poetry in which Job argues with three friends who insist that God always punishes the wicked and rewards the righteous, so Job must have sinned. Job refuses to accept a guilt he does not recognize. His speeches are raw, accusing God of injustice while longing for an advocate or redeemer to vindicate him, and he finally demands that God answer.

God does answer, out of a whirlwind, but not with an explanation. Instead God displays the breadth and strangeness of creation, from the stars to the wild ox to Leviathan, and Job responds with humility. In the epilogue God rebukes the friends for not speaking rightly about him, "as my servant Job has," and restores Job's fortunes. The book refuses simple formulas about suffering while affirming that honest protest addressed to God is a form of faithfulness.
25508: Job is blameless, upright, God-fearing and turning from evil (Job 1:1). The satan is permitted to test him twice (Job 1:12, Job 2:6). Job does not sin or charge God with wrong in the prologue (Job 1:22, Job 2:10). He laments and protests at length (Job 3, Job 6-7, Job 9-10, Job 13-14, Job 16-17, Job 19, Job 21, Job 23-24, Job 26-31), affirming that his redeemer lives (Job 19:25-27). God speaks from the whirlwind (Job 38:1, Job 40:6). Job repents or relents (Job 42:6), God says Job has spoken rightly (Job 42:7-8), and his fortunes are restored (Job 42:10-17). Ezekiel names Job with Noah and Daniel as exemplary righteous men (Ezek 14:14), and James cites his endurance and the Lord's compassion (Jas 5:11).
25509: The Talmud records debate over whether Job was a historical person; one opinion holds he "never existed but was a parable" (b. Bava Batra 15a), while others place him in the days of Moses, the patriarchs, or the return from exile. Some rabbis praise Job's piety; others fault his complaints. Maimonides read the book as a philosophical inquiry into providence (*Guide of the Perplexed* 3.22-23).
25510: Job is venerated as a saint (Orthodox commemoration on May 6) and as a type of Christ the innocent sufferer. Gregory the Great's *Moralia in Job* read the book on literal, allegorical and moral levels, and Job 19:25-27 is used in funeral liturgy as an affirmation of resurrection.
25511: Reformers like Calvin preached extensively on Job as a lesson in submitting to God's hidden providence; many evangelicals read Job 19:25 as anticipating Christ the redeemer, while others note that the Hebrew go'el most naturally means a vindicating kinsman or advocate and leave its referent more open.
25512: Most scholars see a prose frame story (Job 1-2, Job 42:7-17), possibly older, around a poetic core, with Elihu's speeches (Job 32-37) and the wisdom poem (Job 28) often regarded as later additions. The book is commonly dated between the 6th and 4th centuries BC, though earlier dates are defended. It engages a broader ancient wisdom tradition, including the Babylonian *Ludlul bel nemeqi* and the *Babylonian Theodicy*.
